title: The Jobs-Focused Organization
hook: Megan's response times look great until she opens the community survey at 3:22pm.
counterintuition: Organizations that adopt jobs language believe the vocabulary shift is the change. Jobs adoption shows up not in strategy decks but in which standard wins the next difficult tradeoff, under pressure, at handoffs, across functions.
tryThisNow: Name the last decision your team made under pressure. Write one sentence on what governed it. If not the buyer's job, write one sentence on what routing it through the job instead would have cost.
keyTakeaway: A jobs-focused organization is not one that speaks jobs language in strategy decks. It is one whose recurring decisions, under pressure, at handoffs, route choices through the buyer's progress.

breakdown.fastRead:
Megan's dispatch center posts faster response times and calls the quarter a win. The public survey says citizens dial the non-urgent line at 2am during genuine crises because they cannot remember which number to call. The center governs itself by internal speed, not by the public's job: reach the right help fast. Jobs language appeared in the mission statement. Jobs governance did not appear in the decision that kept the two-number system intact.

Training changed the vocabulary. It did not change what governs decisions when the hard tradeoff arrives. The governing standard is not the language on the wall. It is the decision record.
breakdown.deepRead:
Most organizations that adopt jobs thinking make a partial change. They update language in mission statements, strategy decks, and onboarding materials. Then they return to their existing incentive structures, measurement cadences, and compensation formulas. The language is new. The governance is old.

The language-versus-governance split is visible at the moment of a hard tradeoff. Julien stands in a planning meeting where every department has a coherent objection. Traffic will not support the rezoning. Fire access is compromised. The greenspace buffer disappears. Each objection is correct on its own metric. Nobody has been asked to route the decision through the neighborhood's job: a safe, walkable block near the school. The city speaks planning language. It is governed by departmental logic.

Diego's brokerage deployed jobs-centered onboarding six months ago. The renewal process still opens with product comparisons, not job re-confirmation questions. Decision rights for renewals stayed with the product team and its compensation structure. Onboarding speaks jobs language. Renewals are governed by product logic. Training changed vocabulary; it did not change what governs the decisions.

The governance test is practical. Ask: when a decision was made under time pressure last month, which standard actually won? If the answer is consistently a departmental metric, a product roadmap, or a revenue threshold, the organization is jobs-literate, not jobs-focused. Jobs-literate organizations often believe they have completed the transformation. Jobs-focused organizations know the transformation is in the decision record.
breakdown.fullRead:
A jobs-focused organization is built around a recurring decision pattern, not a vocabulary upgrade. The difference is invisible in calm conditions and visible under pressure. When a tradeoff arrives, which standard wins? In most organizations that have adopted jobs thinking, the answer remains: the standard that is measured, compensated, and embedded in the decision structure.

Megan's dispatch center shows this clearly. At 3:22pm, response times are down. A community survey shows citizens calling the non-emergency line during genuine emergencies at 2am because they cannot remember which number to reach. The center governs itself by response efficiency. It does not govern itself by the community's job: reach the right help fast. The two-number system persists not because anyone decided to deprioritize the community's job. The governance structure never asked the question that would have surfaced it.

Julien's rezoning meeting shows the organizational version. Every department objection is internally correct. Traffic analysis says the volume will not work. Fire access standards say the setback is insufficient. Julien asks the question no department was structured to ask: what job is this neighborhood hiring the city to deliver here? The answer, safe, walkable proximity to the school, is absent from every objection. Planning language governs the public materials. Departmental defensibility governs the room.

Diego's brokerage shows the split at a smaller scale. Jobs-centered onboarding was deployed and well received. Six months later, the renewal process still opens with product comparisons. Decision rights for renewals stayed with the product team and its compensation structure. The onboarding change was a language change. The renewal governance was untouched. Training changed what advisors say; it did not change what decides.

Henrik's commercial printing firm ran a successful consulting engagement. Bid win rates improved. A major client departed nine months later. The exit interview was direct: the team talked about their job better than any vendor, then sent proofs back wrong three times and required the client to prove each error. The front end spoke jobs. The production floor optimized proof-cycle cost reduction. Jobs language governed the sale; product logic governed the production.

Kasia's scouting network faces the governance split when the analytics team proposes five standard metrics. A senior scout pushes back: five metrics tell you who runs fastest. The job coaches hire scouts to do is find the player who makes this specific roster better in this specific context. The decision is about which job the network is organized to deliver.

Lin's arts center rebranded successfully for funders and program audiences. Volunteer retention fell. Departing volunteers said they signed up to make something with their hands, not to serve the new mission language. The volunteer's craft job was never represented in the governing standard. A jobs-focused organization routes decisions for every stakeholder through their job. The rebrand was jobs-focused for the primary audience and jobs-blind for the people who kept the programs running.

Jobs governance requires explicit decision rights, not just shared vocabulary. Governance means the job outranks the departmental metric in the moment when they conflict. That is not a language change. It is a structural one.

examples.title: Megan's response times win the quarter while the community job breaks at 2am

planSpec.stakes: internal efficiency metric masks community job failure
planSpec.requiredBeat: response times are down but citizens cannot reach help fast at 2am

examples.scenario: At 3:22pm, Megan reviews the quarterly data: response times are down across the board. She opens a second report, a community survey, and reads that citizens call the non-emergency line during genuine emergencies at 2am because they cannot remember which number to dial. The center is governed by internal response efficiency. The community's job, reach the right help fast, is absent from the decision record. Language says community-centered service. The decision record says internal metrics first. Megan must decide whether to add the community job to the governing standard or accept the gap.
examples.whatToDo: Present both reports together. Frame the board question as which standard governs the center's recurring decisions, and whether that standard matches the community's job.
examples.whyItMatters: A jobs-focused organization is visible in its decision record, not its mission language. If the efficiency report wins and the 2am failure stays unaddressed, the governance pattern has named itself.

examples.title: Julien asks the question every department forgot to ask

planSpec.stakes: coherent departmental objections crowd out the community job
planSpec.requiredBeat: every department is correct on its own metric while the neighborhood job goes unasked

examples.scenario: "Traffic won't support it." "Fire access is compromised." "We lose the greenspace buffer." The planning meeting has run forty minutes. Every department objection is internally coherent. Julien, the city planning director, asks the question nobody asked: what job is this neighborhood hiring the city to deliver here? The room pauses. The answer, a safe, walkable block near the school, is not present in any objection. The city speaks planning language in its public documents. It is governed, in this room, by departmental logic. Julien must decide whether to stop the meeting and reframe the question or let the objection map continue.
examples.whatToDo: Name the job the neighborhood is hiring the city to perform and route each departmental objection through it. The goal is not to override expertise but to give every objection a common reference point.
examples.whyItMatters: Departmental coherence is not jobs governance. When every function is correct on its own metric and the buyer's job goes unasked, the organization is governed by internal defensibility.

examples.title: Diego's onboarding speaks jobs while renewals are still governed by product logic

planSpec.stakes: jobs language in onboarding does not change renewal governance
planSpec.requiredBeat: training changed vocabulary but decision rights for renewals stayed with product compensation

examples.scenario: Jobs-centered onboarding launched six months ago and advisors use the new language well. Diego pulls the renewal queue and opens the first call recording. The advisor leads with product comparisons. The renewal process still opens where it always opened, with the product lineup, not a question about whether the client's job has changed. Decision rights for renewals stayed with the product team and its compensation structure. Onboarding speaks jobs language. Renewals are governed by product logic. Diego must decide whether to escalate the governance gap or absorb it as a training scope problem.
examples.whatToDo: Once Diego confirms that compensation and authority sit with the product team, he should frame the escalation as a governance question rather than a training request. The specific ask is to move one decision: whether to open renewal calls with a job-change question rather than a product-comparison question: across the authority boundary. If that move is blocked, identify the smallest decision point in the renewal path that can be reassigned without restructuring compensation, and start there. The fix is structural: change who owns the opening question in renewals, not how advisors are coached to answer it.
examples.whyItMatters: Training changes what people say. Governance changes what decides. A jobs-focused organization requires both; the renewal process is where the gap between them becomes visible.

examples.title: Henrik's front end speaks jobs while the production floor costs a major client

planSpec.stakes: jobs language in sales does not survive into production governance
planSpec.requiredBeat: client departs because production is governed by cost reduction not the client's job

examples.scenario: The consulting engagement worked. Bid win rates climbed after the front-end sales team learned to speak clients' jobs fluently. Henrik, the account director, watches a major client's account go to zero nine months later. The exit interview is direct: the client said the team understood their job better than any vendor. Then proofs came back wrong three times and each time the client had to prove the error. The front end spoke jobs; the production floor optimized proof-cycle cost reduction.
examples.whatToDo: Extend the jobs governance test into production. Ask which standard governs proof review and error correction. If cost reduction outranks the client's job there, the language change reached only the front door.
examples.whyItMatters: Clients experience the production floor, not the pitch. Jobs language that governs the sale but not the delivery creates a gap the client will eventually name in an exit interview.

examples.title: Kasia's scouting network faces the standardization question

planSpec.stakes: standardization may replace the job the network is actually hired to do
planSpec.requiredBeat: five standard metrics serve a different job than the contextual judgment coaches hire scouts to deliver

examples.scenario: You are Kasia, managing a scouting network asked to standardize. The analytics team has proposed five metrics across every scout in every market. A senior scout pushes back. "Five metrics tell you who runs fastest. The job coaches hire scouts to do is find the player who makes this specific roster better in this specific context. That's not in five numbers." The room divides. You must decide whether to impose the standardization or protect the contextual judgment job. Both choices carry a cost.
examples.whatToDo: Before deciding, name the job coaches hire the scouting network to perform. Test whether the five-metric proposal serves that job or replaces it with a different, more measurable one.
examples.whyItMatters: Standardization serves internal efficiency. Contextual judgment serves the job coaches hire. A jobs-focused organization knows which one it is organized to deliver before imposing a governance change.

examples.title: Lin's rebrand serves funders and loses the volunteers who came to make things

planSpec.domain: community arts center grants and volunteers
planSpec.stakes: jobs governance for primary audience blinds the organization to a different stakeholder's job
planSpec.requiredBeat: rebrand language served funders and audiences but never represented the volunteer's craft job

examples.scenario: The walls are newly painted in the updated brand palette and attendance is up. Lin reads the volunteer exit interviews on a Tuesday morning. Three departing volunteers used nearly the same sentence: they did not sign up to help the community connect creatively. They signed up to make something with their hands. The rebrand language was built for funders and program audiences. The volunteer's craft job was never represented in the governing standard. Lin must decide whether to add the craft job to the governing standard or reframe the rebrand around it.
examples.whatToDo: Map every stakeholder who makes the organization function and name the job each is hiring it to help them do. Build the governing standard to represent all of them.
examples.whyItMatters: A jobs-focused organization routes decisions for every stakeholder through their job. When the volunteer's craft job is absent from the governing standard, the organization is jobs-blind for the people who run the programs.

questions.prompt: A city department posts strong internal efficiency scores while residents report difficulty reaching services in off-hours. The team wants to distinguish organizations that speak jobs language from those whose decisions are actually governed by the job. What does this situation most clearly reveal?
choices: Internal efficiency metrics are the correct governing standard because they can be tracked reliably.
The organization's decision record is governed by internal metrics, not the resident's job, regardless of what its mission language says.
The off-hours problem is an edge case that should be addressed only after the core metric is sustained.
questions.explanation: The gap between strong efficiency scores and residents failing to reach help in off-hours is exactly the language-versus-governance split. The decision record, not the mission statement, reveals which standard actually governs the organization.

questions.prompt: A software team retrained on jobs thinking six months ago. Onboarding materials were updated and advisors use jobs vocabulary in client calls. Renewal rates have not improved. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Twelve to eighteen months is the realistic adoption timeline for jobs language to propagate from onboarding into renewal conversations at scale: new frameworks need repeated use in real client contexts before they change behavior, and the team should hold the current course while tracking leading indicators like the frequency of jobs-language use in recorded renewal calls rather than drawing conclusions from six-month revenue data.
The training changed vocabulary but decision rights in the renewal process stayed with product compensation, leaving the governance unchanged.

Advisors need more structured practice to bridge from vocabulary to behavior: jobs language alone is insufficient, but a combination of role-play simulations, recorded call reviews with coaching, and peer learning sessions would translate the conceptual framework into behavioral change that advisors sustain in real renewal conversations, and that behavior change at scale would eventually reach renewal rates.
questions.explanation: When language changes but renewal governance stays tied to product compensation and decision rights, the organization has completed a vocabulary upgrade, not a governance change. Renewal behavior follows whatever standard controls the actual decision.

questions.prompt: A planning committee has received technically sound objections from four separate departments, each defending its own metric. No department has asked what job the affected community is hiring the city to deliver. What governance problem does this illustrate?
choices: The organization is governed by departmental defensibility rather than a shared jobs standard, so the community job never enters the decision.

The problem is process design: the committee format invites departments to present objections sequentially, creating an advocacy dynamic where each department defends its metric, and restructuring the meeting so departments present a joint pre-reconciled proposal would require them to surface the community job during preparation rather than arriving with unilateral objections.

The problem is insufficient evidence: the committee cannot incorporate the community's job because no department has been tasked with gathering data on what job the neighborhood is hiring the city to deliver, and the governance gap is actually a research gap; once a community needs assessment provides the data, the standard can shift to include it within the existing decision structure.
questions.explanation: When every department is coherent on its own metric but nobody routes the decision through the buyer's job, departmental logic governs. The absence of a shared jobs standard, not lack of expertise, is the problem.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm improves a client's bid win rate by teaching front-end sales to speak jobs language. Nine months later, a major client departs citing repeated production errors and a difficult correction process. How should the firm diagnose this outcome?
choices: Jobs language reached the sale but not the production process, so the client experienced a split between language governance at the front end and operational governance in production.

The diagnosis is a production quality failure independent of jobs governance: the errors that drove the client's departure are a technical execution problem in the proof process, and the root cause analysis should focus on the specific production workflow steps where errors occur, implement quality checkpoints, and establish client-facing error protocols, rather than attributing a technical defect to a language governance question.

The front-end training was insufficient and more precise jobs language at the point of sale would have set accurate client expectations: if sales had been more specific about what the firm's production process could and could not guarantee, the client would have known what correction process to expect, and the departure reflects a mismatch between sales promises and delivery reality that better front-end accuracy would prevent.
questions.explanation: The client experienced the production floor, not the pitch. When jobs language governs the sale but cost reduction governs production, the gap becomes visible at each proof cycle error. The governance split was never addressed by the training.

questions.prompt: An analytics team proposes five standard metrics for a scouting network. A senior scout argues that the job coaches hire scouts to do, finding the player who makes a specific roster better in a specific context, cannot be captured in five numbers. How should the network's leadership frame the decision?
choices: Standardize to five metrics because consistency enables cross-market comparisons that benefit the network's internal reporting.
Name the job the scouting network is actually hired to perform, then test whether the five-metric proposal serves that job or replaces it with a different, more measurable one.
Add two more metrics to the proposal to capture contextual factors and satisfy both the analytics team and the senior scout.
questions.explanation: The governance question is not which option is cleaner internally but which one the clients are hiring the network to perform. Standardization serves an internal efficiency job; the coaches' contextual-fit job may require something the five metrics cannot hold.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit rebrands successfully for funders and program audiences. Volunteer retention falls sharply. Exit interviews show departing volunteers came to make things with their hands, not to serve the new mission language. What does this reveal about the organization's jobs governance?
choices: The rebrand served the primary audience's job but the governing standard never included the volunteer's craft job, making the organization jobs-blind for a stakeholder who keeps programs running.

The volunteer retention problem is a communication gap: the rebrand language was developed for funders and audiences but was not translated for volunteers in terms of how it connects to their hands-on work, and a targeted internal communication campaign reframing the new mission as an expanded context for craft would recover retention by showing volunteers that the rebrand supports rather than replaces the making they came to do.

Volunteer retention volatility after a rebrand is expected because volunteers sort by mission alignment: the departing volunteers self-selected out because their preferences did not match the new positioning, and the organization should survey current volunteers to understand who aligns with the new mission and focus retention investments on that group rather than treating the departure as a structural governance failure.
questions.explanation: When the governing standard is built only around funders and program audiences, the volunteer's craft job goes unrepresented until it surfaces in exit interviews. A jobs-focused organization routes decisions for every stakeholder through their job.

questions.prompt: A leadership team wants to test whether their organization is jobs-focused or merely jobs-literate. Which method most directly answers that question?
choices: Audit the strategy deck and mission statement for jobs vocabulary and count how often the language appears in public materials.
Survey employees on whether they feel the organization has a clear purpose and a strong sense of direction.
Review the last ten decisions made under time pressure and identify which standard, departmental metric, revenue threshold, or buyer's progress, actually governed each one.
questions.explanation: The governing standard is visible in the decision record under pressure, not in language produced during calm planning sessions. Reviewing actual tradeoff decisions reveals whether the job outranked competing standards when it mattered.

questions.prompt: A product manager argues the company is jobs-focused because every strategy presentation uses jobs framing and all teams can articulate the buyer's job clearly. A skeptical colleague pushes back. What is the strongest version of the colleague's objection?
choices: Consistent articulation across all teams is strong evidence of organizational alignment and the skeptic is applying too demanding a standard: most organizations cannot achieve consistent jobs articulation even among senior leaders, so a company where every team can clearly state the buyer's job is operating at a level of alignment that translates into better decisions over time, and demanding governance-level proof at this stage misses what the articulation consistency itself demonstrates.

The colleague's concern is valid but the fix is documentation: requiring that strategy presentations include a section explicitly showing how decisions were evaluated against the buyer's job would make the connection between articulation and choice visible, creating accountability for following the jobs standard, and once documentation becomes standard practice the link between what teams say and what they decide would tighten as leaders review for consistency.

Articulating the buyer's job is necessary but not sufficient. What proves adoption is whether compensation, decision rights, and metric design route choices through that job when it conflicts with departmental goals.
questions.explanation: Articulation is the first stage of jobs thinking. Governance is the second. When decision rights, compensation, and measurement systems still route choices through departmental metrics, the organization has vocabulary adoption but not governance adoption.

questions.prompt: A dispatch center's two-number system persists despite survey evidence that citizens confuse the numbers during genuine emergencies at night. Leadership has reviewed the survey and concluded the response-time metric remains strong. What should be recommended?
choices: The monitoring window should be extended before any action: the survey captured confusion at a single point in time and response-time metrics are trending well, so the recommendation should be to commission a second survey targeting nighttime-only callers in six months, because daytime caller behavior may be creating noise in the confusion rate and a cleaner data set would establish whether the problem is large enough to justify a governance change.

A public education campaign would resolve the confusion without requiring a governance change: if citizens understand the difference between the two numbers through community outreach using clear signage, bill inserts, and social media, the confusion rate drops and the response-time metric is preserved, treating the problem as a communication failure that is addressable without restructuring the decision standard or the two-number system.

Present the governance question directly: the survey shows the current decision standard protects internal efficiency while leaving the community's job, reaching the right help fast, unprotected at the moment that matters most.
questions.explanation: The recommendation needs to name the governance split, not just the data gap. The decision record shows the center is governed by response efficiency. Naming that directly is the step that opens the question of whether the standard should change.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between a jobs-literate organization and a jobs-focused one?
reviewCards.back: A jobs-literate organization uses jobs vocabulary in its strategy materials. A jobs-focused organization routes its recurring decisions, under pressure, at handoffs, across functions, through the buyer's progress. The distinction is visible in the decision record, not the dictionary.

reviewCards.front: How do you test whether an organization is actually governed by the job?
reviewCards.back: Review the last ten decisions made under time pressure. Identify which standard, departmental metric, revenue threshold, product roadmap, or buyer's progress, governed each one. If the buyer's progress did not win the hard tradeoffs, the organization has jobs language but not jobs governance.

reviewCards.front: Why does jobs language in onboarding fail to change renewal behavior?
reviewCards.back: Onboarding changes vocabulary. Renewals are governed by decision rights and compensation structures. If those structures stay anchored to product metrics, the renewal process follows the old governance regardless of what language advisors learned in training.

reviewCards.front: A client departs after praising the sales team. The exit interview mentions production errors. What does this reveal?
reviewCards.back: Jobs language governed the sale; a different standard governed production. The client experienced the production floor. When governance is split between front-end language and back-end operations, the client names the split in the exit interview.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean to route decisions for every stakeholder through their job?
reviewCards.back: Every person who makes the organization function, volunteers, contractors, internal teams, has a job they hired the organization to help them do. A jobs-focused governing standard asks whether each major decision serves or ignores those jobs. Missing one stakeholder's job shows up as unexpected attrition or disengagement.

implementationPlan.title: Identifying the Standard That Actually Governed
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice identifying which standard actually governed a recent decision, not which standard the team would claim in a meeting. The skill is to trace a specific tradeoff back to what won, departmental metric, revenue threshold, or buyer's progress, and name the governance structure that produced that outcome.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team debate reaches a tradeoff between an internal metric and the buyer's progress, then name the governance question out loud before calling a vote: which standard are we letting win here, and is that the standard we want governing this organization?

If a health system or service clearly optimizes for its own administrative convenience over your progress, then name the job you hired it to do and decide whether a substitute better governed by your job is available.
If a volunteer commitment or personal project stops feeling worthwhile, then ask whether the governing standard of the organization you joined still represents the job you hired it to help you do.

If a team or group keeps making decisions that frustrate its intended beneficiaries, then ask whether the group's decision structure is built around the beneficiary's job or around the group's internal metrics.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, identify one decision your organization made last week under real pressure. Write one sentence naming what actually governed that decision. If the answer is not the buyer's job, write one sentence on what it would have cost to route that decision through the job instead.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a recurring process, a renewal, a roadmap review, a hiring decision, and trace its decision rights. Ask who has the authority to let the buyer's job override an internal metric, and whether that person or team is structured to use that authority.

memorableLines.text: Jobs language appeared in the mission statement. Jobs governance did not appear in the decision that kept the two-number system intact.
memorableLines.why: It names the language-versus-governance split in concrete terms the reader can recognize in their own organization.

memorableLines.text: The language-versus-governance split is visible at the moment of a hard tradeoff.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a precise diagnostic moment to watch for, not a vague cultural aspiration.

memorableLines.text: Governance means the job outranks the departmental metric in the moment when they conflict. That is not a language change. It is a structural one.
memorableLines.why: It states the chapter's core argument in its most unambiguous form and raises the bar from vocabulary to structure.
